slides.title: Nine pages, and a table of odds

items.body: "A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution." - the abstract's first sentence

items: Section 11 computes the attacker's catch-up odds
We rerun that computation live, later in this deck

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, announcing on the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list

slides.notes:
STORY (2008-10-31): On 31 October 2008 a pseudonymous author posted nine pages to a cryptography mailing list. Section 11 does something unusual for a systems paper: it computes the attacker's odds. Modelling the race between an honest chain and a secret one as a binomial random walk, it tabulates the probability that an attacker with a share q of the hash power ever catches up from z blocks behind. This deck does not quote that table - it reruns the paper's own procedure and draws the result.
SOURCE: Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' (2008), section 11; announcement of 2008-10-31 on the metzdowd.com cryptography list. The chapter research record reproduced the paper's q=0.1 column - 0.2045873 at one confirmation, 0.0002428 at six - to seven decimal places (examples group AttackerSuccess reruns it for this deck).
slides.take: The paper computes its promises - today we recompute them

slides.title: Change comes back to you
slides.sub: Inputs are spent whole, like banknotes

items.label: the fee is the remainder - computed, not quoted

items.cap: the fraction table, from the owner's 2025 deck

slides.notes:
SAY: Making change is the practice of adding to a transaction an output that returns the surplus to the person who is paying. The book explains the need with money in a shop: if you buy a five-dollar item with a twenty-dollar bill you expect fifteen dollars back, and in the same way a transaction input, like a currency note, cannot be partly spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Pay a 20-lira coffee with a 50-lira note: where is the change output?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 2 - MakingChange, TransactionFee.
slides.lede: A 100,000-satoshi output pays a 75,000 bill the way a banknote pays a coffee: spent whole, with change coming back - minus the tip to the miner.
slides.take: Inputs are spent whole; the difference returns as change

slides.title: Fees price bytes, not value
slides.sub: Block space is the scarce good

items: A block holds bytes, not value - space is what runs out
So fees are bid per virtual byte, not per coin moved
This transaction: 143 vbytes, 5,000 sat - about 35 sat/vB

items.label: 2 - the rate a wallet actually bids

slides.notes:
SAY: The fee rate is the fee a transaction pays for each unit of the space it takes in a block. Miners do not compare transactions by their total fee alone; they divide the fee by the size of the transaction, as a shopper divides the price of a bag of rice by its weight to find the best deal.
ASK: Why does moving 1 BTC cost the same as moving 100?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 2 - FeeRate, TransactionSize.
slides.take: You pay for block space - size, not amount

slides.sub: No postmaster - transactions travel by gossip

slides.title: Five free bitcoins for every visitor

items.cap: Gavin Andresen - photo: Stephen McCarthy / Web Summit, CC BY 2.0

items: June 2010: almost nowhere to buy bitcoin existed
Andresen stocked a website with 1,100 BTC of his own
Five coins free per visitor; a CAPTCHA was the only price
Thousands got their first coins - then came the exchanges

items.who: Gavin Andresen, the developer Satoshi later handed the project to
items.where: freebitcoins.appspot.com, announced on the bitcointalk forum

slides.notes:
STORY (2010-06-11): In June 2010 there was almost nowhere to buy bitcoin, so a developer in Massachusetts stocked a website with 1,100 of his own coins and gave five to anyone who asked - solving a CAPTCHA was the only price. Thousands of people got their first bitcoin from Gavin Andresen's faucet. The giveaway seeded the user base the first exchanges and the first payments then grew from, and Andresen went on to lead Bitcoin's development when Satoshi withdrew in 2011.
SOURCE: Andresen's own announcement thread, bitcointalk.org topic 141, 2010-06-11: 'Get 5 free bitcoins from freebitcoins.appspot.com', initially stocked with 1,100 BTC. Photo: Web Summit 2014, CC BY 2.0.
slides.take: Before exchanges, distribution itself had to be invented

slides.title: A transaction's journey to everyone
slides.sub: Gossip, hop by hop, until every mempool holds it

items: No central dispatcher - the whisper network is the mail
Bob sees it unconfirmed within seconds
It waits in mempools until a miner picks it

slides.notes:
SAY: Transaction propagation is the spread of a signed transaction across the network until it has reached, in practice, everyone who cares, including the miners who may record it. It is the composition of the two previous concepts: the wallet transmits the transaction to some node, and then the gossip rule carries it onward hop by hop.
ASK: What happens if two conflicting spends gossip at once? (next section answers)
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 2 - TransactionPropagation, Mempool.
slides.take: Four seconds of gossip puts Alice's payment in every mempool

slides.notes:
SAY: A block is the unit in which transactions are added to the blockchain. The chapter says that transactions are bundled into blocks, and that blocks have a very small header that must be formed in a very specific way, requiring an enormous amount of computation to get right but only a small amount to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why hash the header only, not the whole megabyte?

slides.title: One root for a thousand leaves
slides.sub: The Merkle tree pins every transaction at once

items: Hash the transactions in pairs, then pairs of pairs
One root remains - 32 bytes for any number of leaves
Change any leaf and the root betrays it instantly

rows: L = [d(x) for x in (b'A', b'B', b'C', b'D')]
items.label: four leaves to one root, computed

slides.notes:
SAY: A merkle tree, also called a binary hash tree, is a structure for summarizing and verifying the integrity of large sets of data. The book defines it as a tree constructed by hashing paired data, the leaves, then pairing and hashing the results until a single hash remains, the merkle root, and notes that in Bitcoin the leaves are almost always the transactions of a single block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: A light client holds only the root - what must a proof hand it?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 2 - MerkleTree.
slides.take: Change any leaf and the root betrays it

slides.title: The coinbase: where new coin enters
slides.sub: The one transaction with no inputs

items.label: the reward at this block, computed
inputs in a coinbase - the only transaction so allowed

slides.notes:
SAY: The coinbase transaction is the special first transaction of every block, by which the miner pays itself. The book's glossary calls it the first transaction in a block, always created by a miner, and the mining chapter adds the distinguishing property: unlike regular transactions the coinbase transaction does not consume unspent outputs as inputs, but has only one input, called the coinbase input, which implicitly contains the block reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Trace any coin backwards: where must the trail always end?

slides.take: Every coin in existence began life in a coinbase

slides.title: The day someone printed 184 billion bitcoin

items.label: BTC conjured by one transaction in block 74,638
from forum report to Satoshi's 0.3.10 fix

rows.label: output of 92,233,720,368.54 BTC - overflow, summed as a small number
0.3.10's corrected rule: outputs must sum in range - chain rebuilt without them

items.who: An unknown attacker; spotted by developer Jeff Garzik; patched by Satoshi Nakamoto
items.where: block 74,638, discussed live on the bitcointalk forum

slides.notes:
STORY (2010-08-15): On 15 August 2010 block 74,638 contained a transaction paying out about 184,467,440,737 BTC - thousands of times the 21 million cap. Two outputs were so large that, summed as 64-bit integers, they overflowed to a small number and slipped past the checks. Jeff Garzik flagged the 'strange block' on the forum within the hour; Satoshi shipped version 0.3.10 with a corrected rule about five hours after the block, and the honest chain, rebuilt without the forged coins, overtook the bad one. The 184 billion bitcoins ceased to exist.
SOURCE: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Value_overflow_incident: block 74,638 of 2010-08-15 (two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54 BTC each), Garzik's 'Strange block 74638' thread, Satoshi's 0.3.10 patch ~5 hours later, good chain ahead by block 74,691.
slides.take: Validation by every node is the immune system - it worked

slides.title: Confirmations: depth, not time
slides.sub: Each block on top multiplies the attacker's bill

items: A confirmation is a block on top of yours - depth, not minutes

slides.notes:
SAY: A confirmation is a block that commits to a transaction, counted once for the block that contains it and once more for each block built on top.

slides.title: Semantics and practice
slides.sub: The chapter as data, and the chapter on your laptop
slides.notes:
SAY: This branch reads the chapter with the eyes of the course rather than of the book. A transaction chain, as the first branch described it, is a record of what came from what: each output exists because a transaction consumed earlier outputs, and each transaction happened because somebody who held a key authorized it.
